catalog_citation: Kari, Ethelbert Emmanuel. 2017. Central Delta languages: An overview. Stellenbosch Papers in Linguistics 47: 1-26. doi:10.5774/47-0-213 (open access; Ogbrọnụagum tone data cited from Kari, Ethelbert E. 2000. Ogbronuagum (the Bukuma language). LINCOM Europa, p. 9)
catalog_locator: Sec. 3.4 'Tone', p. 11, incl. Table 7 'Tones in Central Delta languages', Ogbrọnụagum column (Kari 2000:9); saved file
catalog_quote: 3.4 Tone Alex (1989:24) remarks that “all Central Delta lects operate a basic two-tone system”. These tones are low tone, which is marked with a grave accent ( ̀), and high tone, which is marked with an acute accent ( ´). There is also a downstep phenomenon in these languages. The downstep is marked with a small arrow pointing downwards ( ꜜ) between two high-toned syllables. Apart from the syllabic nasal, tone in these languages is anchored on vowels. Table 7 shows these tones and downstep as found in Abuan, Oḍual and Ogbrọnụagum. [Table 7: Tones in Central Delta languages ... Ogbrọnụagum (Kari 2000:9): éɡù “fear”, èɡú “louse”, òníꜜní “one”] Like in lexical items, tone can distinguish grammatical constructions in Central Delta languages.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (extracted text of the saved open-access PDF, Kari 2017, SPiL 47:1-26, doi:10.5774/47-0-213). The quoted passage is at sec. 3.4 'Tone', p.11 (the text layer) word for word: 'Alex (1989:24) remarks that "all Central Delta lects operate a basic two-tone system". These tones are low tone.. high tone.. There is also a downstep phenomenon in these languages.. Apart from the syllabic nasal, tone in these languages is anchored on vowels. Table 7 shows these tones and downstep as found in Abuan, Odual and Ogbronuagum.' Table 7's Ogbronuagum column (Kari 2000:9) gives egu 'fear' (H-L), egu 'louse' (L-H), oni(downstep)ni 'one', exactly as the first reader's bracketed summary says. I read sec.…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Ogbronuagum is described as a lexical/grammatical tone language with two level tones (H, L) plus downstepped H, tone-bearing units being vowels and syllabic nasals; the source (by the author of the only published grammar sketch of the language) makes no statement about word stress or accent at all.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress; tone also marks grammatical distinctions (illustrated for Odual statement vs question).
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical tone on citation forms (minimal triplet) and grammatical tone; no word- or phrase-level stress domain discussed. Statement is in a family overview but the Ogbronuagum data are the author's own (Kari 2000:9).
new_statements.identity_note: Kari 2017 treats Ogbronuagum (Ogbrọnụagum, the language of Bukuma village near Buguma, Degema LGA, Rivers State; ~12,000 speakers) = Glottolog ogbr1243 / ISO ogu; the tone data are from Kari's own 2000 LINCOM sketch of the same variety. No dialect differentiation is reported. Note Kari 2017 calls Alex 1987 a 'BA long essay' whereas Glottolog lists it as an MA thesis.

sources.note: Sec. 3 'Phonological overview' covers vowels, consonants, syllable/morpheme structure and tone (3.4, p.11): Central Delta languages incl. Ogbronuagum have a basic two-tone system (H, L) with downstep, tone anchored on vowels and syllabic nasals; Table 7 gives an Ogbronuagum tonal minimal triplet (egu 'fear' HL / egu 'louse' LH / onini 'one' L-H-downstep-H) citing Kari 2000:9. The words stress/accentual/prominence/intonation do not occur anywhere in the paper. Author is the same linguist who wrote the primary Ogbronuagum sketch (Kari 2000).
Stub; no phonology; cites only Ethnologue.
